sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You've tried four different AI-in-editor setups over the past seven lessons. This final lesson synthesizes everything into a practical decision framework — and ends with a commitment: pick your primary setup for the rest of this course.

## The Four Options

**Option 1: VS Code + Continue.dev (free, any model)**
- Cost: Free — you pay only for API usage (or use local Ollama models at zero cost)
- Setup: Install the extension, configure a model in `config.json`
- Best for: Students who want to use Claude or other models without a GitHub subscription; anyone who wants to run AI locally for privacy; maximum model flexibility
- Limitation: Autocomplete quality depends on the model you choose; no multi-file composer

**Option 2: VS Code + GitHub Copilot (GitHub subscription)**
- Cost: Free tier available; $10/month Copilot Pro for unlimited use
- Setup: Install two extensions, sign in with GitHub
- Best for: Developers already using GitHub; those who want the most polished autocomplete experience; anyone doing code review or PR workflows
- Limitation: Tied to GitHub's model choices (though Copilot now lets you select Claude/GPT)

**Option 3: Cursor (free tier generous)**
- Cost: Free tier (monthly fast-request budget); $20/month Pro
- Setup: Download and install; imports VS Code settings automatically
- Best for: Building multi-file projects; anyone who finds the Composer workflow faster than writing prompts piecemeal; more complex codebases
- Limitation: Sends code to Cursor's servers by default (Privacy Mode available); separate app from VS Code

**Option 4: Windsurf (free tier)**
- Cost: Free tier (credit-based); paid plans available
- Setup: Download and install; imports VS Code settings
- Best for: Those who prefer Cascade's real-time visual feedback; anyone who found Windsurf more intuitive in lesson 6-7
- Limitation: Smaller community than Cursor; less third-party documentation

## Decision Matrix

Use this table to evaluate each option against your specific situation:

| Factor | VS Code + Continue | VS Code + Copilot | Cursor | Windsurf |
|--------|--------------------|-------------------|--------|----------|
| **Cost** | Free (+ API) | Free tier / $10/mo | Free tier / $20/mo | Free tier |
| **Setup effort** | Medium (config file) | Low (sign in) | Low (import from VS Code) | Low (import from VS Code) |
| **Autocomplete quality** | Model-dependent | Excellent | Excellent | Excellent |
| **Multi-file editing** | No | No | Yes (Composer) | Yes (Cascade) |
| **Model choice** | Any (Claude, local, etc.) | GitHub's selection | Claude + GPT-5 | Codeium + Claude |
| **Data privacy** | Configurable | Microsoft/GitHub | Privacy Mode available | Privacy Mode available |
| **Best use case** | Flexibility, local AI | GitHub-integrated work | Complex projects | Visual, agent-driven work |

For the rest of this course — primarily building web projects and working with APIs — **any option works**. The difference becomes meaningful when you're working on larger projects later in the course (Parts 13–14).

**Recommendation for most students:** Start with **VS Code + GitHub Copilot** (free tier) for the rest of this course. It requires the least configuration, has the most documentation and community support, and the free tier is sufficient for everything in Parts 6–12. When you reach Part 13 (building a complete project), revisit this decision — Cursor's Composer becomes significantly more valuable when you're working across many files simultaneously.

**You can switch at any time.** Your code lives in your project folder — it's not locked to any editor. Cursor, Windsurf, and VS Code can all open the same folder. Trying a different tool for a week costs nothing and takes 5 minutes. Don't over-optimize this decision now.

sections.title: Pick Your Setup and Document Your Choice
sections.content:
This workshop has two parts: a decision and a commitment.

**Part 1 — Fill in the matrix**
Open `notes/prompt-experiments.md` (or create a new file `notes/editor-setup-decision.md`) and paste this table:

```
| Factor       | VS Code + Continue | VS Code + Copilot | Cursor | Windsurf |
|--------------|--------------------|-------------------|--------|----------|
| Cost         |                    |                   |        |          |
| Setup effort |                    |                   |        |          |
| My experience|                    |                   |        |          |
| My score /5  |                    |                   |        |          |
```

Fill in the "My experience" row based on what you actually felt using each tool in lessons 6-1 through 6-7. Score each one from 1–5 for how much you enjoyed using it.

**Part 2 — Write your commitment**
Below the table, write one sentence in this format:

```
For this course and beyond, I'm going to primarily use _____ 
because _____.
```

Examples:
- *"For this course and beyond, I'm going to primarily use VS Code + Copilot because I already have a GitHub account and the autocomplete just works."*
- *"For this course and beyond, I'm going to primarily use Cursor because I liked being able to generate multiple files at once."*
- *"For this course and beyond, I'm going to primarily use VS Code + Continue because I want to use Claude as my model and keep data off Microsoft's servers."*

Save the file. This is your decision. You're committing to reduce tool-switching friction — not choosing forever.

sections.title: Workshop A — Personal AI Editor Assessment
sections.content:
Make a data-driven decision about your AI editor setup based on your actual experience.

**Step 1 — List the editors you have tried** (even briefly): VS Code + Copilot, Continue.dev + Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, or others.

**Step 2 — For each editor**, rate from 1-5 on:
- Code quality produced
- Understanding of my existing code
- Speed (how fast it responds and implements)
- Review experience (how easy to see and accept changes)
- Setup effort
- Cost

**Step 3 — Ask Claude:** *"Based on these ratings [paste your matrix] and my work profile [describe: language, task types, team size], what AI editor setup would you recommend? Explain the reasoning."*

**Step 4 — Identify your "must have" vs "nice to have" features.** What would make you switch editors?

**Step 5 — Write a one-paragraph decision.** Your AI editor setup, why you chose it, and when you'll revisit the decision.

sections.title: Workshop B — Hybrid AI Editor Setup
sections.content:
Many developers use more than one tool. This workshop designs a hybrid setup where each tool serves its best use case.

**Step 1 — Identify your 4 most common AI coding tasks:**
- Task type 1: [e.g., "write new functions from spec"]
- Task type 2: [e.g., "review AI-generated code"]
- Task type 3: [e.g., "debug runtime errors"]
- Task type 4: [e.g., "refactor existing code"]

**Step 2 — For each task**, decide: which AI tool would you use?

**Step 3 — Ask Claude:** *"I want a hybrid AI editor setup using [your chosen tools]. For each of my task types [list them], which tool should I use and why? Identify any tasks where my tool choice might be wrong."*

**Step 4 — Document your hybrid workflow** as a short reference:
```
## My AI Editor Workflow
- New features: [tool + how]
- Code review: [tool + how]
- Debugging: [tool + how]
- Refactoring: [tool + how]
```

**Step 5 — Commit to this workflow for 4 weeks.** After 4 weeks, review: which parts worked? What would you change?

sections.title: Workshop C — Cost vs Quality Analysis
sections.content:
AI editor costs vary significantly. This workshop helps you maximise value for your specific situation.

**Step 1 — Research current pricing** for each AI editor option:
- GitHub Copilot Individual
- Cursor Pro
- Windsurf Pro
- Claude API via Continue.dev (pay-per-use)
- Free tiers of each

**Step 2 — Estimate your monthly usage:** How many hours per week do you code? What percentage involves AI assistance?

**Step 3 — Ask Claude:** *"Help me compare the cost-effectiveness of these AI editor options for a developer who codes [X] hours/week with [Y% AI assistance]: [list your options with their pricing]. What's the most cost-effective setup?"*

**Step 4 — Factor in the value:** What is one hour of your time worth? If an AI editor saves you 30 minutes/day, how does that compare to its monthly cost?

**Step 5 — Make a decision:** Is the cost of the tool you want justified? Write your conclusion.

sections.title: Workshop D — Build Your AI Coding Workflow Document
sections.content:
A documented workflow is the foundation of consistent, high-quality AI-assisted coding.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude to help you write your workflow document:**
```
Help me create an "AI Coding Workflow" document for my personal reference. I use [your tools] for [your work type].

The document should cover:
1. How I start a new coding task (planning, speccing before coding)
2. How I write code with AI assistance (tools, prompts, review process)
3. How I review AI-generated code (checklist, mandatory steps)
4. How I debug with AI help (process, what info to provide)
5. How I commit and document (commit messages, code documentation)
6. Red lines — things I never let AI do without full understanding
```

**Step 2 — Personalise every section** with your specific tools, prompts, and practices.

**Step 3 — Add your review checklist** at the end: the mandatory steps before accepting any AI-generated code.

**Step 4 — Mandatory meta-review:** Ask Claude: *"Review this workflow document. What important practices are missing? What common AI coding mistakes does this workflow not protect against?"*

**Step 5 — Save and use:** This document is your operating manual for AI-assisted development.

sections.question: You are comparing Cursor ($20/month) and using Claude API via Continue.dev (pay-per-use). What information do you need to make a cost-effective decision?
options: Just compare the monthly subscription costs
Estimate how many API calls you make per month to calculate Continue.dev costs, then compare to Cursor's flat rate considering both price and which produces better output for your work
Always choose the more expensive option — it will be higher quality
sections.explanation: Cost-effectiveness requires knowing both the total cost of each option AND the value difference. Calculate: how many tokens you use per day × Claude API rates × days/month = monthly Continue.dev cost. Compare to Cursor's flat rate. If they're similar, quality and workflow fit become the deciding factor. Flat rates favor heavy users; pay-per-use favors occasional users. Neither is universally better.

sections.question: A colleague says "I just use whichever AI coding tool is trending on social media." What is the problem with this approach?
options: Trending tools are usually poorly tested
Tool choice should be based on which tool produces the best output for your specific language, task type, and workflow — not popularity
Popular tools are always the most expensive
Trending tools change too frequently to learn properly
sections.explanation: The best AI coding tool for you depends on factors specific to your work: your programming language, your primary task types (building vs reviewing vs debugging), your team's tool chain, your budget, and how you naturally think about code. A tool that benchmarks well or trends on Twitter may be mediocre for your specific context. Use the data from your own experience — not others' preferences.

sections.content: **Part 6 complete.** You've gone from zero to a fully configured AI-assisted coding environment. You know how Copilot autocomplete works, how to use Copilot Chat for explanations and debugging, what Continue.dev offers as a free alternative, how Cursor's Composer handles multi-file edits, and what makes Windsurf's Cascade different. You've picked your setup. In Part 13, you'll leave the extension ecosystem behind and learn Claude Code — a terminal-based AI agent that can read, edit, and reason about entire projects.
